sanity_expectations: At g = 0, the formula should return H_g = H0 exactly for all sampled H0, Ne, mu, and fixed sigma.
For fixed H0, Ne, and sigma, increasing mu should raise long-generation heterozygosity and separate late-g curves above zero rather than toward zero.
For fixed H0, mu, and sigma, smaller Ne should generally produce faster early heterozygosity loss than larger Ne.

Because g also appears inside the Ne modulation, H_g versus g should not be a single shared exponential family across all g; departures from constant semilog relaxation are most visible when g/(2Ne) is not tiny.
For fixed Ne, mu, g, and sigma, higher H0 should yield higher H_g, with the H0 contrast strongest at early-to-intermediate generations and reduced after long relaxation.

H0: claimed-input/time axis -> independent variable (confirmed by freedom metadata: sampled static input, not a time axis)
Ne: claimed-input/time axis -> independent variable (confirmed by freedom metadata: sampled static input, not a time axis)
g: claimed-input/time axis -> independent variable (confirmed by structure and context: elapsed-generation sampling axis in an explicit mapping)

sigma: claimed-parameter -> parameter (confirmed by freedom metadata and explicit static role)
spec.rationale: Structural analysis shows no derivatives, integrals, delays, or auxiliary dynamics: this is a static algebraic mapping for H_g as a function of H0, Ne, g, mu, and sigma, so the equation type is explicit and should be sampled directly. Because the record has explicit freedom metadata with freedom_change='none', preserve the declared static V/P design: H0, Ne, g, and mu remain sampled inputs and sigma remains a fixed parameter. The chosen ranges expose the intended contrasts without collapsing to recovery limits. H0 spans low to high initial diversity so the H0-dependent transient curvature remains visible. Ne spans small to moderately large finite populations so drift modulation by g/(2Ne) is visible at low-to-intermediate Ne but not everywhere deep in the weak-drift regime. g extends from 0 to 300 generations to include the parent-reference condition g=0 exactly and enough later generations to reveal bending away from a single homogeneous decay law. mu is weak-to-moderate and strictly below 1/2, avoiding biologically implausible values while allowing the mutation-supported positive plateau and exact-(1-2mu)^2 effects to be visible; the lower bound is not so tiny that all mutation effects vanish over the sampled horizon. Sigma is fixed at an appreciable but bounded value to keep the excess inbreeding correction active without driving denominators toward singularity or making the system unrealistically extreme. Exact noiseless input-output pairs should be generated by direct evaluation of the explicit expression.

spec.scenario_text: Replicate finite populations begin with a specified heterozygosity at a neutral biallelic locus. Random sampling of parental gene copies causes lineages to share ancestors, progressively reducing expected heterozygosity across generations. The benchmark predicts the replicate-mean heterozygosity from the initial value, effective population size, and elapsed number of generations. Population size and all other background conditions remain constant within each sampled case.

response_change.parent_relation: H_g = H0*(1 - 1/(2*Ne))**g gives monotone exponential decay of expected heterozygosity toward 0, determined only by H0, Ne, and g under a closed population.
response_change.child_relation: Add recurrent mutation so the mapping still decays with g but approaches a positive mutation-drift balance instead of 0, with the approach rate depending jointly on Ne and mutation strength.
response_change.observable_effect: At fixed H0 and Ne, long-run heterozygosity no longer tends to zero; small populations still lose diversity quickly at first, but for sufficiently large g the curve flattens above zero, unlike the parent.

plan.activation_condition: Observable when mutation is not negligible over the sampled horizon, roughly when the cumulative per-lineage mutation opportunity across generations is comparable to drift loss; most visible at larger g and finite Ne, while over very short times the child reduces nearly to the parent.
plan.train_hidden_contrast: In training ranges with moderate g the child already shows slightly slower late-time decline than a pure exponential; in holdout with larger g the same mechanism becomes clearer through a nonzero plateau rather than continued collapse toward 0.
plan.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the zero-mutation limit.
plan.promotion_reason: The baseline inputs cannot distinguish a closed finite population from one with recurrent mutation. A mutation-rate input is needed because the new target mapping changes across cases with different mutation intensities; it cannot be inferred uniquely from H0, Ne, and g alone.
plan.gap_statement: The current model omits recurrent mutation, so it forces all replicate-mean heterozygosity trajectories to decay toward zero in every case.
plan.baseline_assumption: Mutation, migration, and selection are absent.
plan.scientific_mechanism: Forward and backward mutation at a neutral biallelic locus reintroduce alternative alleles, opposing fixation by drift and creating a positive equilibrium heterozygosity.
plan.rationale: The parent response is a single closed-population decay shape: for fixed H0, increasing g always pushes H_g exponentially toward 0, with Ne only stretching the decay timescale. A realistic next refinement is to relax the no-mutation assumption by allowing recurrent mutation, which changes the scored target mapping itself, not just an auxiliary trajectory. Vary mutation rate across cases while holding H0 and Ne fixed: the child predicts that late-generation heterozygosity levels separate, with higher mutation sustaining more diversity and eventually producing a positive asymptote. The parent with one shared parameterization cannot reproduce this cross-condition contrast, because all of its trajectories converge to 0 and differ only by the existing H0, Ne, and g dependence. The effect is scientifically admissible when mutation is weak but nonzero and generations are numerous enough for mutation input to accumulate; if the sampled g is too small or mutation is extremely rare, the distinction may be hard to see, and the child should smoothly collapse back toward the parent in that regime.

plan.scientific_mechanism: Exact symmetric two-state mutation changes heterozygosity through the full Bernoulli transition factor rather than its first-order truncation, altering the generation-to-generation retention factor and equilibrium under moderate recurrent mutation.

plan.activation_condition: Observable when the reproduction system departs from random mating enough that identity-by-descent rises faster than the Wright-Fisher random-union prediction, while mu is not so large that mutation dominates drift; practically, finite to moderate Ne and multi-generation observations are needed so curvature beyond a single exponential is visible.
plan.train_hidden_contrast: In training, the same mechanism appears as systematically steeper heterozygosity loss at small-to-moderate g for some finite-Ne cases than the parent’s one-factor decay allows; in holdout, the contrast extends to larger g where the altered relaxation curvature and shifted equilibrium remain inconsistent with one shared parent parameterization.
plan.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the random-mating limit where excess inbreeding/selfing tends to zero, so the standard Wright-Fisher heterozygosity recursion with recurrent symmetric mutation is restored.
plan.gap_statement: The current model treats finite-population drift as if parental union is fully random, collapsing all ancestry structure into Ne and omitting excess identity generated by partial selfing or equivalent inbreeding structure.
plan.baseline_assumption: The parent assumes random mating/random union of gametes so that drift reduces heterozygosity only through the standard Wright-Fisher factor 1 - 1/(2*Ne).
plan.scientific_mechanism: Partial self-fertilization or mating among relatives increases homozygosity beyond pure random-sampling drift, modifying expected heterozygosity decay under otherwise neutral recurrent mutation.
plan.rationale: A realistic next refinement is to relax the parent’s random-mating assumption rather than add an unrelated process. The parent target mapping is a fixed-environment shortcut: once Ne and mu are given, all cases share one generation-to-generation retention factor and therefore one specific decay curvature from H0 toward equilibrium. In many finite populations, however, reproduction can include partial selfing or excess related matings, which is scientifically distinct from merely lowering Ne because it changes how identity accumulates relative to the Wright-Fisher closure used in the parent derivation. Varying g while holding H0, Ne, and mu fixed, the child mechanism predicts faster early heterozygosity loss and altered relaxation curvature; under admissible conditions with appreciable inbreeding and finite observation horizons, a single parent parameter set cannot reproduce both this steeper initial decline and the later mutation-limited saturation across those conditions. This is a changed target mapping, not merely a hidden auxiliary trajectory, because the scored quantity H_g itself changes as a function of the supplied inputs. The limitation is that if mating is effectively random, or if mutation is so strong that drift/inbreeding effects are masked, the refinement collapses back toward the parent and may not be empirically distinguishable.

plan.activation_condition: Observable when elapsed generations are long enough that cumulative drift is non-negligible, g/Ne is not tiny, and the underlying demographic trend across those generations is sustained rather than rapidly reversing; strongest at low to moderate mu where mutation does not mask drift curvature.
plan.train_hidden_contrast: Training may mostly sample near-stationary cases where a constant-Ne approximation is adequate, while holdout can include longer horizons or stronger demographic trend so that heterozygosity loss departs systematically from a single homogeneous decay shape.
plan.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the limit of zero demographic trend, where generation-specific effective size becomes constant and the cumulative decay collapses to the current constant-Ne form.
plan.gap_statement: The current model treats effective population size as constant over the entire observation window, collapsing all drift history into one fixed Ne even though realistic finite populations often experience sustained growth or decline that changes the cumulative heterozygosity loss rate with generation.
plan.baseline_assumption: Effective population size is constant across generations.
plan.scientific_mechanism: Time-inhomogeneous genetic drift under deterministic demographic change modifies the cumulative probability that two sampled gene copies avoid recent coalescence, altering the generation dependence of expected heterozygosity decay even under neutrality and recurrent mutation.
plan.rationale: A realistic next refinement is to relax the parent's time-homogeneous drift assumption rather than adding an unrelated process. The parent target mapping uses one constant Ne to set the full H_g-versus-g shape, so once H0, mu, and sigma are fixed, changing g only moves along a single decay family with fixed curvature. The scientific gap is that demographic history within the elapsed interval can change drift strength across generations. Under sustained decline, later generations experience stronger drift than early ones, making heterozygosity loss accelerate relative to the parent's single-scale prediction; under sustained growth, the opposite occurs. This is a changed target mapping, not merely an auxiliary reinterpretation, because the observable output H_g itself changes for the same supplied H0, nominal Ne, mu, sigma, and g when the constant-Ne assumption is relaxed to a nonstationary demographic history. The contrast is visible by varying g while holding H0, mu, and sigma fixed: the parent predicts one homogeneous relaxation shape, whereas the child predicts systematically different curvature over g once cumulative drift exposure is redistributed across generations. This matters when g spans enough generations for drift to accumulate and when mutation is not so strong that it dominates the trajectory. Limitation: with freedom_change constrained to none, the immediate refinement must be encoded as a changed assumption using existing symbols rather than introducing an explicit new demographic-trend input, so the eventual implementation will need to represent nonstationary drift in a reduced way.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed Ne, mu, and sigma, expected heterozygosity decays with generation through a single time-homogeneous retention scale, so the H_g-versus-g curve has one effective relaxation shape set globally by the same drift term.
response_change.child_relation: Replace the constant effective population size assumption by deterministic generation-dependent effective size under sustained demographic change, so the cumulative loss rate is governed by a nonstationary product/integral over per-generation drift strengths. The target then depends on how g interacts with the demographic trend, changing the curvature of H_g across generations even when initial and current scales are comparable.
response_change.observable_effect: Holding H0, mu, and sigma fixed, populations with the same nominal Ne but observed over longer g show faster-than-parent early loss under sustained decline or slower-than-parent early loss under sustained growth; the curvature of heterozygosity decay over g is no longer captured by one global relaxation constant.

contract.activation_condition: Observable when elapsed generations are long enough that cumulative drift is non-negligible, g/Ne is not tiny, and the underlying demographic trend across those generations is sustained rather than rapidly reversing; strongest at low to moderate mu where mutation does not mask drift curvature.
contract.train_hidden_contrast: Training may mostly sample near-stationary cases where a constant-Ne approximation is adequate, while holdout can include longer horizons or stronger demographic trend so that heterozygosity loss departs systematically from a single homogeneous decay shape.
contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the limit of zero demographic trend, where generation-specific effective size becomes constant and the cumulative decay collapses to the current constant-Ne form.
contract.scientific_mechanism: Time-inhomogeneous genetic drift under deterministic demographic change modifies the cumulative probability that two sampled gene copies avoid recent coalescence, altering the generation dependence of expected heterozygosity decay even under neutrality and recurrent mutation.
contract.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient-only correction because g now changes the drift scale inside the nonlinear retention law itself, coupling elapsed time with baseline Ne and altering curve shape rather than just rescaling one constant rate.
contract.assumption_before: Effective population size is constant across generations.
contract.assumption_after: Effective population size entering drift-mediated heterozygosity loss is modulated by elapsed generations as a reduced approximation to sustained demographic change.
contract.parent_reduction: Setting g = 0 makes Ne*(1 + g/(2*Ne)) = Ne and recovers the parent expression exactly.
contract.observable_signature: Holding H0, mu, and sigma fixed, populations with the same nominal Ne but observed over longer g show curvature in H_g versus g that bends away from the parent's single homogeneous decay family because drift strength is internally modulated by g through 1/(2*Ne*(1 + g/(2*Ne))); this effect is most visible when elapsed generations are long enough that cumulative drift is non-negligible, g/Ne is not tiny, and mutation is low to moderate.
contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this pattern across short and long g simultaneously because in the parent all g dependence enters through one fixed drift scale set by constant Ne, whereas here g also changes that scale internally. Retuning Ne or sigma can shift one overall relaxation rate but cannot create the specific cross-g curvature change induced by the multiplicative Ne-g modulation.

domain_mechanisms.description: finite capacity, resource limitation, or saturation

baseline_mechanisms: Random sampling of gene copies between generations
Increasing identity by shared ancestry in a finite population
baseline_assumptions: The locus is neutral and biallelic.
Effective population size is constant across generations.
Mutation, migration, and selection are absent.
The target is an expectation over replicate populations rather than one stochastic realization.
scientific_constraints: Expected heterozygosity must remain between zero and one half for a biallelic locus.
Expected heterozygosity cannot increase with elapsed generations under the baseline conditions.
Increasing effective population size cannot accelerate the expected loss of diversity.
Zero initial heterozygosity would remain zero.
refinement_agenda: Add mutation that replenishes allelic diversity.
Allow time-varying effective population size, including bottlenecks.
Introduce migration from a genetically differentiated source.
Add linked selection that changes local effective ancestry.
Predict the variance among replicate populations in addition to the mean.

response_change.parent_relation: H_g = H0*(1 - 1/(2*Ne))**g gives monotone exponential decay of expected heterozygosity toward 0, determined only by H0, Ne, and g under a closed population.
response_change.child_relation: Add recurrent mutation so the mapping still decays with g but approaches a positive mutation-drift balance instead of 0, with the approach rate depending jointly on Ne and mutation strength.
response_change.observable_effect: At fixed H0 and Ne, long-run heterozygosity no longer tends to zero; small populations still lose diversity quickly at first, but for sufficiently large g the curve flattens above zero, unlike the parent.

evolution_contracts.activation_condition: Observable when mutation is not negligible over the sampled horizon, roughly when the cumulative per-lineage mutation opportunity across generations is comparable to drift loss; most visible at larger g and finite Ne, while over very short times the child reduces nearly to the parent.
evolution_contracts.train_hidden_contrast: In training ranges with moderate g the child already shows slightly slower late-time decline than a pure exponential; in holdout with larger g the same mechanism becomes clearer through a nonzero plateau rather than continued collapse toward 0.
evolution_contracts.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the zero-mutation limit.
evolution_contracts.promotion_reason: The baseline inputs cannot distinguish a closed finite population from one with recurrent mutation. A mutation-rate input is needed because the new target mapping changes across cases with different mutation intensities; it cannot be inferred uniquely from H0, Ne, and g alone.
evolution_contracts.domain_mechanism: mutation-driven saturation toward a finite drift-mutation equilibrium
evolution_contracts.scientific_mechanism: Forward and backward mutation at a neutral biallelic locus reintroduce alternative alleles, opposing fixation by drift and creating a positive equilibrium heterozygosity.
evolution_contracts.difficulty_rationale: The added input mu changes the asymptote of the H0, Ne, g mapping, producing a saturation surface over generations rather than the parent's single zero-limit decay family. This cannot be mimicked by a coefficient-only correction because the child adds an observable nonzero long-run limit across mutation conditions.
evolution_contracts.assumption_before: Mutation, migration, and selection are absent.
evolution_contracts.assumption_after: Mutation is allowed and supplies recurrent allelic input, relaxing the closed no-mutation assumption while keeping neutrality and constant population size.
evolution_contracts.observable_signature: Vary mutation rate across cases while holding H0 and Ne fixed: the child predicts that late-generation heterozygosity levels separate, with higher mutation sustaining more diversity and eventually producing a positive asymptote. The parent with one shared parameterization cannot reproduce this cross-condition contrast, because all of its trajectories converge to 0 and differ only by the existing H0, Ne, and g dependence.
evolution_contracts.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce the new signature because, for every admissible H0, Ne, and g, the parent family always approaches 0 as g increases. Retuning existing coefficients only changes the decay timescale or initial scaling; it cannot create a mutation-dependent positive plateau across cases with one shared formula.

response_change.parent_relation: For fixed Ne and mu, expected heterozygosity decays toward a mutation-drift equilibrium as a single geometric factor raised to g, so the log-decay rate is constant across generations.
response_change.child_relation: Allow the recurrent-mutation contribution to use the exact two-allele transition factor (1-2*mu) multiplying the drift term, replacing the linearized mutation effect. This preserves the same variables but changes the g-dependence from a first-order approximation to a slightly different geometric curvature at moderate mu.
response_change.observable_effect: When Ne is held fixed and mu varies into the non-negligible range, the heterozygosity trajectory versus g bends differently: the exact model decays slightly more slowly and approaches a different equilibrium than the linearized parent, with the contrast accumulating over many generations.

evolution_contracts.activation_condition: Observable when mutation is not asymptotically tiny relative to 1/g, so that O(g*mu^2) corrections accumulate over the sampled generations; especially with moderate g and nonzero mu while Ne remains fixed.
evolution_contracts.train_hidden_contrast: In training, small but nonzero mu already perturbs the decay rate and equilibrium; in holdout with larger g or somewhat larger admissible mu, the mismatch from the parent's first-order mutation approximation becomes more visible as a systematic curvature difference.
evolution_contracts.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the weak-mutation limit mu -> 0 to first order, where (1-2*mu) and the parent's linearized mutation treatment coincide up to higher-order terms.
evolution_contracts.domain_mechanism: exact symmetric two-allele mutation combined with finite-population drift
evolution_contracts.scientific_mechanism: Exact symmetric two-state mutation changes heterozygosity through the full Bernoulli transition factor rather than its first-order truncation, altering the generation-to-generation retention factor and equilibrium under moderate recurrent mutation.
evolution_contracts.difficulty_rationale: This is structurally harder than a coefficient-only correction because the exact mutation law changes the saturation level and the geometric retention factor simultaneously through nonlinear mu dependence, so one shared parent parameterization cannot match both early-generation slope and long-generation plateau across varying mu.
evolution_contracts.assumption_before: Per-generation mutation acts only through a weak-mutation linear approximation in the heterozygosity recursion.
evolution_contracts.assumption_after: Per-generation mutation follows the exact symmetric two-allele transition law before drift, yielding the full nonlinear mutation contribution to heterozygosity.
evolution_contracts.parent_reduction: In the weak-mutation limit mu -> 0 to first order, the child expression reduces to the parent up to O(mu**2) differences.
evolution_contracts.observable_signature: Holding H0 and Ne fixed while increasing mu from very small to moderate admissible values, the child predicts a different saturation scale and a slightly different geometric curvature in H_g as a function of g: the discrepancy is negligible near mu=0 but accumulates over many generations, whereas the parent enforces one linearized mutation-dependent decay law.
evolution_contracts.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this contrast across varying mu because its mapping ties both transient decay and asymptotic heterozygosity to the same first-order mutation dependence. Retuning existing parameters may fit one mu regime or one generation range, but it cannot simultaneously match the exact mu-dependent plateau and the altered g-curvature generated by the (1 - 2*mu)**2 retention factor over the stated activation conditions.

response_change.parent_relation: With constant Ne and symmetric mutation, H_g is a single exponential relaxation from H0 to one mutation-drift equilibrium, so the log-retention and approach-to-equilibrium curvature are fixed once Ne and mu are fixed.
response_change.child_relation: Relax the idealized random-union assumption by allowing partial self-fertilization/inbreeding already implicit in finite-population reproduction, which changes the effective heterozygosity retention factor nonlinearly relative to the census-scale Ne description and thus alters the g-dependence curvature of H_g even at fixed H0, Ne, and mu.
response_change.observable_effect: Across generations, heterozygosity decays faster at early and intermediate g than predicted by the parent’s single retention factor, while still approaching a mutation-drift balance; the parent cannot match both the initial slope and later saturation curvature with one shared parameter set if data include cases where inbreeding-induced identity is appreciable.

evolution_contracts.activation_condition: Observable when the reproduction system departs from random mating enough that identity-by-descent rises faster than the Wright-Fisher random-union prediction, while mu is not so large that mutation dominates drift; practically, finite to moderate Ne and multi-generation observations are needed so curvature beyond a single exponential is visible.
evolution_contracts.train_hidden_contrast: In training, the same mechanism appears as systematically steeper heterozygosity loss at small-to-moderate g for some finite-Ne cases than the parent’s one-factor decay allows; in holdout, the contrast extends to larger g where the altered relaxation curvature and shifted equilibrium remain inconsistent with one shared parent parameterization.
evolution_contracts.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the random-mating limit where excess inbreeding/selfing tends to zero, so the standard Wright-Fisher heterozygosity recursion with recurrent symmetric mutation is restored.
evolution_contracts.domain_mechanism: bounded excess identity-by-descent in finite populations
evolution_contracts.scientific_mechanism: Partial self-fertilization or mating among relatives increases homozygosity beyond pure random-sampling drift, modifying expected heterozygosity decay under otherwise neutral recurrent mutation.
evolution_contracts.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient-only correction because the parent's random-mating drift factor is replaced by a bounded saturation law in Ne for the excess inbreeding contribution, so the target mapping changes its curvature across population-size regimes rather than only shifting one constant multiplier.
evolution_contracts.assumption_before: The parent assumes random mating/random union of gametes so that drift reduces heterozygosity only through the standard Wright-Fisher factor 1 - 1/(2*Ne).
evolution_contracts.assumption_after: Excess inbreeding/selfing adds a bounded, saturating contribution to identity-by-descent, reducing the per-generation heterozygosity retention factor beyond the random-mating Wright-Fisher term.
evolution_contracts.parent_reduction: Setting sigma=0 removes the excess inbreeding correction and exactly restores the parent expression.
evolution_contracts.observable_signature: Parent: for fixed H0, Ne, and mu, g maps to one specific exponential relaxation set by (1 - 1/(2*Ne))*(1 - 2*mu)**2. Child: for the same H0, Ne, and mu, excess inbreeding lowers retention by sigma/(1 + 2*Ne), a saturating finite-capacity correction that is strongest at finite Ne and weakens as Ne grows, producing steeper early decline and a lower mutation-drift saturation level. This is observable when identity-by-descent from non-random mating is appreciable and multi-generation H_g values are sampled.
evolution_contracts.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this contrast across admissible conditions because the parent ties all finite-population curvature to one random-mating retention factor, whereas the child introduces an additional bounded Ne-dependent loss channel from inbreeding. Refitting existing parent parameters can mimic one portion of the trajectory, but not simultaneously preserve the same H0, Ne, and mu interpretation while matching both the steeper early decline and the shifted long-run saturation over cases where excess inbreeding is active.

response_change.parent_relation: For fixed Ne, mu, and sigma, heterozygosity decays as a single exponential approach to one equilibrium with a generation-independent retention factor, so log-distance to equilibrium is linear in g.
response_change.child_relation: Replace the generation-independent excess-inbreeding effect with a heterozygosity-dependent inbreeding impact, so the effective retention factor changes as H_g changes; this bends the trajectory versus g and alters how mutation opposes inbreeding at low versus high heterozygosity.
response_change.observable_effect: Across cases with the same Ne, mu, and sigma but different H0, the parent predicts the same normalized decay shape in g, whereas the child predicts stronger early excess loss when heterozygosity is high and weaker excess loss as diversity becomes depleted.

diagnostic_groups.name: inbreed_load
diagnostic_groups.role: current constant excess heterozygosity-loss contribution from selfing/inbreeding

evolution_contracts.activation_condition: Most visible when sigma is appreciable and mutation is not so strong that the system is pinned near its mutation-drift equilibrium; practically, intermediate g and contrasting H0 values away from that equilibrium reveal the curvature change.
evolution_contracts.train_hidden_contrast: In training, the mechanism appears as different transient shapes across H0 at fixed Ne and sigma; in holdout, the same dependence extends to larger sigma or longer g where the parent's single exponential shape becomes more visibly inadequate.
evolution_contracts.continuation_path: In the limit where the heterozygosity dependence of the excess-inbreeding effect vanishes, the child reduces to the parent's constant-sigma retention law.
evolution_contracts.scientific_mechanism: Identity correlations created by selfing/consanguinity can saturate as loci become homozygous, making the marginal inbreeding-driven loss of heterozygosity weaker when H is already low than when many individuals remain heterozygous.
evolution_contracts.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient-only correction because the excess-inbreeding coefficient now depends on the evolving heterozygosity level itself, so the scored mapping is no longer a shared single-exponential family in g and acquires H0-dependent curvature.
evolution_contracts.assumption_before: The current model assumes the extra heterozygosity loss from selfing or related mating is a constant per-generation decrement factor independent of the current heterozygosity level.
evolution_contracts.assumption_after: The excess inbreeding/selfing penalty is state dependent and scales with current heterozygosity, so its marginal effect saturates as homozygosity accumulates.
evolution_contracts.parent_reduction: For vanishing state dependence of the inbreeding term, the heterozygosity-dependent correction disappears and the law returns to the parent single-retention-factor form.
evolution_contracts.observable_signature: Hold Ne, mu, and sigma fixed and compare low versus high H0. The parent gives the same normalized approach-to-equilibrium curve in g for both, but the child gives a steeper initial decline from high H0 and a later flattening once heterozygosity has been depleted, with the contrast strongest for appreciable sigma and intermediate g.
evolution_contracts.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this because its log-distance to equilibrium has constant slope in g for all H0 at fixed Ne, mu, and sigma. Refitting H0, Ne, mu, or sigma globally only changes amplitude, equilibrium, or one shared exponential rate, not the H0-dependent curvature generated by a state-dependent inbreeding coefficient.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed Ne, mu, and sigma, expected heterozygosity decays with generation through a single time-homogeneous retention scale, so the H_g-versus-g curve has one effective relaxation shape set globally by the same drift term.
response_change.child_relation: Replace the constant effective population size assumption by deterministic generation-dependent effective size under sustained demographic change, so the cumulative loss rate is governed by a nonstationary product/integral over per-generation drift strengths. The target then depends on how g interacts with the demographic trend, changing the curvature of H_g across generations even when initial and current scales are comparable.
response_change.observable_effect: Holding H0, mu, and sigma fixed, populations with the same nominal Ne but observed over longer g show faster-than-parent early loss under sustained decline or slower-than-parent early loss under sustained growth; the curvature of heterozygosity decay over g is no longer captured by one global relaxation constant.
